the window always opens with only Project open.

At the left end of the bar, left of the tab bar itself rather than inside it, so the tab bar's own padding and bottom line don't reach it, sits the left container. It holds, in order, the project indicator, the collapse chevron, and the activity spinner, and can hold other things after them. It is the same whether the ribbon is expanded, beside the tabs, or collapsed, leading the row of primary co

Everything in it is vertically centred in that height, with no gap between one thing and the next and no padding around them: each thing's own size is all the room it takes. The container shrinks to fit what it holds, and when it holds nothing, it isn't there at all.

At the right end of the bar, right of the tabs, or of the primary commands when the ribbon is collapsed, sits the right container. It holds nothing yet, and can hold other things. It lays out what it holds as the left container does: vertically centred, with no gap between things and no padding around them, shrinking to fit, and not there at all while it holds nothing, as it is now.

### Shape

#### Description

A form titled "New Project", with a close button, holding the project's name, where it goes, the template it starts from, and its Belay options, and along the bottom a "Cancel" button and a primary "New" button that creates it. The name field has focus when the form opens.

#### Layout

The form's body is two columns of equal width side by side, top aligned, scrolling together when the panel is too short for them. The first holds the project itself: its name, its location, the Git checkbox, and the spec, code, and shape roots. The second holds what it starts from and what it's written for: the template, then the agents.

#### Name

A "Name" field for the project's name, which is also the name of its folder. It can't be empty, contain a slash or backslash, or be "." or "..".

#### Location

A "Location" row showing the folder the project's folder goes in, with a "Browse…" button beside it. It starts in the folder holding the open project, or the user's home folder when no project is open. Beneath it, muted, the full path of the folder that will be created.
Browse opens a [FolderBrowserScope](../../ui/components/folder-browser/index.md#folder-browser-scope) in place of the form, titled "Choose where the project goes" and starting in the current location. A new folder for the project to go in can be created from there. Choosing a folder makes it the location, and choosing or cancelling goes back to the form, just as it was left.

#### Git

Beneath the location, an "Initialize a Git repository" checkbox, checked to start with. Its label is shown in full, like the agents' labels.

#### Templates

At the top of the second column, a "Template" group lists the templates a project can start from, one row each, in order, as radio buttons, only one chosen at a time: each shows the template's name, and beneath it, muted, what it holds. The first is chosen to start with. There are two:

- "Base", with nothing more than the project needs: an empty index.pi in the spec root
- "Scope, concept, and shape", which seeds the spec root with a lib of the abstract scope, concept, and shape anchors a spec is written with, each in a file of its own, an index.pi in the lib exporting them all, an index.pi in the spec root using the lib, and an example scope, with its concept and shape, to start from

The templates are folders in the project-templates folder at the root of the Suspense repository, one per template, and are built into the application when it is built, so changing or adding one changes what the next build offers. Each holds a template.json giving its name, its description, and its place in the order, and, in a spec folder, the files it seeds the spec root with, laid out as they a

#### Agents

Beneath the template, in the second column, an "Agents" group of checkboxes, one per agent Belay has an adapter for, each with the directory it writes into: "Claude Code" (.claude), "OpenCode" (.opencode), and "Codex" (.codex). Only Claude Code starts checked. At least one must be checked.
Each checkbox's label is shown in full beside it, vertically centred on it, with room below its baseline so the bottoms of letters like p and y, and of the brackets, are never cut off.

#### Folders

Three fields, each a path relative to the project folder: "Spec root", starting as ./spec; "Code root", starting as ./src; and "Shape root", starting as ./spec/shape, which can be left empty to go without one. Spec root and code root can't be empty. A path is written with a leading ./ whether or not it was typed with one, and none can be absolute or climb out of the project with "..".

##### Overview

The input and buttons live inside the body of a tab bar, a flat strip 32 pixels tall on the ribbon's command area colour, #222222 in dark mode, with no line anywhere in it, whether beneath it, between its tabs, or around them. Each tab is only its label, in small text, with 8 pixels to each side of it and no border, and its label is always in its mode's colour at full strength, of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope), whether selected or not: Code red, Chain's icon purple, Spec blue, Ask green, and Freeform grey. The one exception is Chain selected, when Code and Spec take Chain's purple too, as the chain says. The selected tab is marked only by its background, the sa
The chat input starts in the combined mode: Chain is selected, so Code and Spec are selected together, and a prompt sent before switching tabs changes the code and the spec together. Each open project keeps the tab it was left on, as the [OpenProjectsScope](../../open-projects/index.md#open-projects-scope) says, so a project starts on Chain the first time it is opened in a launch, and switching back to it selects the tab it was on.
Pressing <Ctrl+Tab> while in the chat input cycles from Code to Chain to Spec to Ask to Freeform and back to Code, <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> the other way, and focus remains in the chat input. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too, not <Cmd>.
<Tab> and <Shift+Tab> don't switch tabs, and don't indent the text either. They move keyboard focus out of the chat input to the next or previous control, as they do everywhere else. While the completion menu is open, <Tab> is still the menu's.

##### Chain

Chain is a tab with unusual behaviour. It shows an icon rather than a label, reading "Code and Spec" as its tooltip, and selecting it selects both Code and Spec. Its icon is drawn in Chain's colour, the purple of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope), selected or not, as every tab's label is in its mode's colour. It never shows a focus outline, and its icon looks evenly spaced between Code and Spec whichever of the two is selected.
Unselected, it shows a broken chain dimmed to 50% opacity, and sits between Code and Spec like any other tab, overlapping neither of them.
Chain, like every tab, has no line along its bottom or sides, in combined mode or separate, since the tab bar draws no lines at all. Nothing draws a line beneath Chain and then hides it, since a hidden line can show again wherever rounding to the display's pixels uncovers it.
Selected, it shows a joined chain at full opacity. Selecting it animates as though it took a margin of -50% of its own width on both its left and right sides: Code and Spec slide together until they meet underneath it, so it ends up sitting on top of both. Deselecting it animates them apart again. While Chain is selected, Code and Spec both show as selected, one continuous background beneath the two of them and Chain, reading as a single unified tab. Chain itself has a transparent background, so the joined Code and Spec show through underneath it.
While Chain is selected, the Code and Spec labels are drawn in Chain's purple, the same colour as its icon, rather than red and blue, so the unified tab reads as one mode in one colour. Their colour follows the slide: as Code and Spec slide together, their labels shift from red and blue to purple, and as they slide apart they shift back, each reaching its own colour as the tabs settle.

##### Help
#### Creating

"New" is disabled, with a tooltip saying why, until the name is valid, the paths are, and an agent is checked, and while a project is being created. A field that isn't valid says why beneath it once something has been typed in it.
Pressing it creates the project's folder, and any folders leading to it, then writes piton.config.pi there, creates the spec root, writes the chosen template's files into it, or an empty index.pi when the template gives none, and creates the code root and any shape root. It never overwrites anything: a folder that already holds a piton.config.pi is refused, a file already in the spec root is left 
With "Initialize a Git repository" checked, once the rest is created the project's folder is made a Git repository with `git init`, unless it already is the top of one, and a .gitignore is written there ignoring what Suspense keeps for this machine alone rather than for the project, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says. An existing .gitignore is left as it is
Once created, the project opens as if opened with the [OpenProjectScope](../project/open-project/index.md#open-project-scope), becoming the [ProjectDirectoryScope](../project-directory/index.md#project-directory-scope), and the form closes. If anything fails, the form stays open and says what went wrong above its buttons.

use /lib
use /ui
from /scope/new-project import NewProjectScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/ask-conversation import AskConversationScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/chat-input import ChatInputScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/modes import PromptModesScope
from /scope/user-preferences import UserPreferencesScope
from /scope/welcome import WelcomeScope
from /ui/components/ribbon/application-tab import RibbonApplicationTabScope
from /ui/components/ribbon/project-tab import RibbonProjectTabScope

export ui-component WalkthroughScope:
    concept: {WalkthroughConcept}

concept WalkthroughConcept:
    pitch:
        A guided walkthrough that takes a new user from nothing to a project
        of their own, then through the prompt modes one by one, pointing at
        each part of the window as it explains it, so the first prompt is
        sent knowing what each mode does.

    shape: {WalkthroughShape}

shape WalkthroughShape:
    description:
        The walkthrough is a series of steps, each pointing at one part of
        the window with a spotlight and explaining it in a callout. It never
        sends a prompt or changes anything but what the user does at its
        bidding, as creating the project, and what it selects to show, as a
        ribbon tab or a chat input tab.

    spotlight:
        While a step shows, the window is dimmed, as an inset panel dims it,
        but for a cut-out around the part the step points at, with 4 pixels
        of room and corners rounded 6 pixels, outlined in the theme's accent,
        so that part reads as lit. The cut-out moves to each step's part,
        easing between them over 200 milliseconds, and follows it if the
        window is resized.

        Beside it sits the callout, a card on the theme's raised surface with
        corners rounded 8 pixels, a border, and a shadow, at most 320 pixels
        wide, placed on whichever side of the part has room, with a small
        pointer toward it, and never off the window. It holds the step's
        title, its text as a paragraph or two, "Step N of M", muted, and
        along its bottom a Back button, disabled on the first step, a primary
        Next button, reading "Done" on the last step, and a "Skip tour" link
        at the left. It is drawn in the theme's roles, in dark mode and
        light.

        Only the callout and the part lit take the mouse while a step
        shows: clicks on the dimmed window do nothing, so the walkthrough is
        never left by accident. <Escape> skips the tour, as Skip tour does,
        and <Enter>, while Next is enabled, goes to the next step.

    steps:
        The steps, in order, each selecting what it points at before it
        shows, as opening the Project tab of the ribbon, expanding the ribbon
        first if it is collapsed:

        - "Projects live here", the Project tab of the ribbon, opened: a project is a folder holding its spec, its code, and a piton.config.pi that says where each is, and everything Suspense does, it does in the project open.
        - "Create a project", the New Project button of the @{RibbonProjectTabScope}: it asks for the project to be created. Next is disabled, and the step goes on by itself once the New Project form opens, as clicking the button opens it. Where a project is already open, the callout also offers "Use the open project", which skips to the prompt modes with it.
        - "Fill it in", the New Project form, as the @{NewProjectScope} says, lit whole, the callout beside the panel, above it: it names the project, where it goes, the template it starts from, and the agents it is written for, and says the defaults are a fine start. Next is disabled; the step goes on by itself once the project is created and opens. Cancelling the form goes back to the step before.
        - "Every prompt has a mode", the tabs of the @{ChatInputScope}: what is typed below is sent in the mode of the tab selected, and each mode does a different kind of work.
        - "Code", the Code tab, selected: changes the code to do what the prompt asks, reading the spec to know how, and leaves the spec as it is. Code tasks run on this machine, in the project.
        - "Spec", the Spec tab, selected: changes the spec, the description of what the application should be, and leaves the code as it is, so a change can be agreed on before anything is built. Spec tasks run in a container that holds only the spec, and the spec is built after each.
        - "Code and Spec", the Chain tab, selected, Code and Spec together: changes the spec first, then hands it to a code step that changes the code to match, one prompt doing both. It is where the chat input starts, and the usual way to ask for a change.
        - "Ask", the Ask tab, selected: asks a question about the code and the spec, changing neither, and answers beside the tasks, as the @{AskConversationScope} shows; questions run straight away, never waiting behind tasks.
        - "You're ready", the chat input's text box: type a prompt, pick its mode, and send it. The walkthrough can be taken again from Walkthrough, in the Application tab.

        Each mode's step reads in that mode's colour, its title and its
        outline, as the @{PromptModesScope} colours it. Back goes to the
        step before, selecting again what it selects, but never back into
        the steps that create the project once it has been created.

    ending:
        Done, on the last step, ends the walkthrough, leaving the chat input
        on the Chain tab, as it starts, with keyboard focus in its text box.
        Skip tour ends it straight away, at any step, leaving everything as
        it is. Either way the dimming goes, and the walkthrough is remembered
        as taken for the user, as the @{UserPreferencesScope} says, so it is
        never offered again by itself.

    starting:
        The walkthrough starts by itself only once for a user, until it has
        been taken or skipped: when the @{WelcomeScope}'s Get started is
        pressed, or, where the welcome page doesn't open at launch because
        everything is ready, once the window has opened. It can be taken
        again at any time with the Walkthrough command, a "Walkthrough"
        button with a signpost icon in the Help group of the
        @{RibbonApplicationTabScope}, after Welcome, whose tooltip says it
        walks through creating a project and the prompt modes. It is a full
        button, and not primary. Started with a project open, it starts at
        its first step all the same, offering "Use the open project" at the
        second.

        It never starts over an inset panel, but waits for it to close, and
        it isn't offered while work is running; started from its command, it
        closes any inset panel open first.

export ui-component WelcomeScope:
    concept: {WelcomeConcept}

concept WelcomeConcept:
    pitch:
        A welcome page that checks what Suspense needs is installed and
        working, says plainly what isn't, and guides each fix, so Suspense
        is ready before the first prompt is sent rather than failing on it.

    shape: {WelcomeShape}

shape WelcomeShape:
    description:
        Shown in an @{InsetPanelScope}, as the settings are, headed "Welcome
        to Suspense", with a close button whose tooltip says it closes the
        welcome page. Beneath the heading, a muted line says that Suspense
        runs coding harnesses on a project's code and spec, and checks here
        that what it needs is in place. Then a checklist, one row per check,
        in order, and at its foot a "Check again" button, and a line saying
        whether Suspense is ready.

    checks:
        Each check is a row: a status icon, a green check when it passes, a
        red cross when a required check fails, an amber warning when an
        optional one does, and a spinner while it is being checked; the
        check's name; muted beside it what was found, as the version a
        command reports; and, beneath, while it fails, a line of guidance
        saying what is wrong, why Suspense needs it, and how to fix it, with
        the action that fixes it where Suspense can take one. The checks go
        in this order.

        - "Git", found by running `git --version`, required, since projects
            are git repositories. Missing, its guidance links to
            https://git-scm.com/downloads.
        - "Piton", found by running `piton --version`, required, since the
            spec is built, sliced, and checked with it. Missing, its guidance
            links to https://github.com/piton-lang/piton-rs.
        - "Harness", the harness in use, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope}
            says, found by running its command with `--version`, required,
            since Code tasks run it on the host. Missing, its guidance names the
            command and links to the harness's installation instructions,
            https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/setup for Claude Code,
            https://github.com/openai/codex for Codex, and
            https://opencode.ai/docs/ for OpenCode, with a "Choose another
            harness" button that opens the Agent section of the
            @{SettingsWindowScope}.
        - "Podman", found by running `podman --version`, required, since
            Spec tasks, a Chain prompt's spec steps, and questions run in a
            container, as the @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says. Missing, its
            guidance links to Podman's installation instructions for the
            platform, as it gives them.
        - "Podman machine", on macOS and Windows only, required, passing
            while a Podman machine is running. With none, its guidance offers
            "Set up Podman", and with one stopped, "Start Podman", each as the
            @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says, what the command prints shown
            beneath the row as it runs. It is checked only once Podman is
            found, and shows "Needs Podman", muted, until then.
        - "Containers", required, passing once Podman runs a container for
            the application, as by running `podman info`. Failing, its guidance
            says Podman couldn't be accessed, with what Podman printed, as the
            @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says. It is checked only once the
            checks above it pass.
        - "Harness login", required, passing while the harness in use is
            logged in in its container, read from its volume. Not logged in,
            its guidance offers "Log in", which shows the login view, as the
            @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says. It is checked only once
            "Containers" passes.

        Every check runs in the background, all at once where they don't
        wait on one another, as each command is run without a console
        window, never holding up the window. A command that takes longer
        than 10 seconds fails its check, saying it didn't answer.

    ready:
        Suspense is ready when every required check passes, and the line at
        the checklist's foot then reads "Suspense is ready", with a
        "Get started" button that closes the welcome page; otherwise it
        reads how many checks still need attention, as "2 things need
        attention", and Get started is not shown, the close button closing
        the page all the same, since what passes still works.

        "Check again" runs every check anew. A check whose action, as setting
        up Podman or logging in, finishes runs again by itself, and so do the
        checks waiting on it. A link opened in the browser leaves the page as
        it is, until Check again.

    opening:
        At each launch, Suspense runs the checks in the background as it
        starts. If any required check fails, the welcome page opens over the
        main window once they are done, unless the user has turned off
        "Show at launch when something needs attention", a checkbox at the
        page's foot, on until turned off, remembered for the user. When
        every check passes, nothing is shown. It opens by itself at most
        once in a launch: once it has been closed, or the user has opened
        anything else in the inset panel meanwhile, nothing opens it again
        but the Welcome command, not checks run again, not a fix finishing,
        and not checks still failing.

    closing:
        The welcome page closes as any inset panel does, as the
        @{InsetPanelScope} says: with its close button, its Get started
        button, <Escape>, or a click on the dimmed window around it, and
        always, whatever its checks say, failing, passing, or still running,
        and however it was opened. Closing it never waits on a check, nor on
        a fix still running, as setting up Podman, which carries on in the
        background, its check running again once it finishes without opening
        the page. Once it closes, focus goes back to the chat input, and
        everything beneath it works as it does with the page closed, what
        needs a failing check failing as it says it does.

        It can be opened at any time with the Welcome command, a "Welcome"
        button with a checklist icon in a "Help" group, the last group of the
        @{RibbonApplicationTabScope}, after Preferences, whose tooltip says it
        checks that Suspense is ready to run. It is a full button, and not
        primary, so the collapsed ribbon leaves it out. Opening it runs every
        check anew. It needs no project, and works the same with or without
        one.

    description:
        The Application tab of the ribbon, last of the tabs.

    groups:
        appearance:
            An "Appearance" group holds the Brightness command, its one
            control; there is no Dark mode switch, since the slider reaches
            both modes.

        colours:
            A "Colours" group, between Appearance and Preferences, holds the
            Theme command.

        preferences:
            A "Preferences" group holds the Settings command.

        help:
            A "Help" group, the last, after Preferences, holds the Welcome
            command, then the Walkthrough command.

    commands:
        brightness:
            A "Brightness" slider, which runs the whole interface from its
            darkest to its lightest: a moon icon, then a horizontal slider
            120 pixels wide, then a sun icon, with nothing showing the setting
            as a number. As a ribbon setting, it has no background of its
            own, and sits straight on the commands' area, as tall as a slim
            button. Its tooltip says it makes the whole interface darker or
            lighter, from its darkest to its lightest, keeping its contrast,
            and that double-clicking it resets it.

            Its one track runs through every appearance the @{ThemeScope}
            allows, darkest first: dark mode from its darkest brightness to
            its lightest, then light mode from its darkest to its lightest,
            one position for each step, with no switch between them. So all
            the way left is dark mode at its darkest, and all the way right
            light mode at its lightest; dragging past dark mode's lightest
            step changes the window to light mode, and back.

            Dragging it changes the mode and the brightness straight away as
            it moves, and once it is let go saves the mode showing and each
            mode's brightness among the @{UserPreferencesScope}. A mode that
            can't be saved shows a notification titled

            saved fails quietly. Its thumb follows the appearance showing,
            however that was changed, such as from the palette, but not while
            it is being dragged.

            mode showing back to its brightness at 0, keeping the mode, and
            saves it; the second click doesn't also move the thumb.

            It is primary, so the collapsed ribbon keeps it: its icons and
            track as they are, only as wide as they are, as tall as a small

export ui-component WalkthroughScope:
    concept: {WalkthroughConcept}

concept WalkthroughConcept:
    pitch:
        A guided walkthrough that takes a new user from nothing to a project
        of their own, then through the prompt modes one by one, pointing at
        each part of the window as it explains it, so the first prompt is
        sent knowing what each mode does.

    shape: {WalkthroughShape}

shape WalkthroughShape:
    description:
        The walkthrough is a series of steps, each pointing at one part of
        the window with a spotlight and explaining it in a callout. It never
        sends a prompt or changes anything but what the user does at its
        bidding, as creating the project, and what it selects to show, as a
        ribbon tab or a chat input tab.

    spotlight:
        While a step shows, the window is dimmed, as an inset panel dims it,
        but for a cut-out around the part the step points at, with 4 pixels
        of room and corners rounded 6 pixels, outlined in the theme's accent,
        so that part reads as lit. The cut-out moves to each step's part,
        easing between them over 200 milliseconds, and follows it if the
        window is resized.

        Beside it sits the callout, a card on the theme's raised surface with
        corners rounded 8 pixels, a border, and a shadow, at most 320 pixels
        wide, placed on whichever side of the part has room, with a small
        pointer toward it, and never off the window. It holds the step's
        title, its text as a paragraph or two, "Step N of M", muted, and
        along its bottom a Back button, disabled on the first step, a primary
        Next button, reading "Done" on the last step, and a "Skip tour" link
        at the left. It is drawn in the theme's roles, in dark mode and
        light.

        Only the callout and the part lit take the mouse while a step
        shows: clicks on the dimmed window do nothing, so the walkthrough is
        never left by accident. <Escape> skips the tour, as Skip tour does,
        and <Enter>, while Next is enabled, goes to the next step.

    steps:
        The steps, in order, each selecting what it points at before it
        shows, as opening the Project tab of the ribbon, expanding the ribbon
        first if it is collapsed:

        - "Projects live here", the Project tab of the ribbon, opened: a project is a folder holding its spec, its code, and a piton.config.pi that says where each is, and everything Suspense does, it does in the project open.
        - "Create a project", the New Project button of the @{RibbonProjectTabScope}: it asks for the project to be created. Next is disabled, and the step goes on by itself once the New Project form opens, as clicking the button opens it. Where a project is already open, the callout also offers "Use the open project", which skips to the prompt modes with it.
        - "Fill it in", the New Project form, as the @{NewProjectScope} says, lit whole, the callout beside the panel, above it: it names the project, where it goes, the template it starts from, and the agents it is written for, and says the defaults are a fine start. Next is disabled; the step goes on by itself once the project is created and opens. Cancelling the form goes back to the step before.
        - "Every prompt has a mode", the tabs of the @{ChatInputScope}: what is typed below is sent in the mode of the tab selected, and each mode does a different kind of work.
        - "Code", the Code tab, selected: changes the code to do what the prompt asks, reading the spec to know how, and leaves the spec as it is. Code tasks run on this machine, in the project.
        - "Spec", the Spec tab, selected: changes the spec, the description of what the application should be, and leaves the code as it is, so a change can be agreed on before anything is built. Spec tasks run in a container that holds only the spec, and the spec is built after each.
        - "Code and Spec", the Chain tab, selected, Code and Spec together: changes the spec first, then hands it to a code step that changes the code to match, one prompt doing both. It is where the chat input starts, and the usual way to ask for a change.
        - "Ask", the Ask tab, selected: asks a question about the code and the spec, changing neither, and answers beside the tasks, as the @{AskConversationScope} shows; questions run straight away, never waiting behind tasks.
        - "You're ready", the chat input's text box: type a prompt, pick its mode, and send it. The walkthrough can be taken again from Walkthrough, in the Application tab.

        Each mode's step reads in that mode's colour, its title and its
        outline, as the @{PromptModesScope} colours it. Back goes to the
        step before, selecting again what it selects, but never back into
        the steps that create the project once it has been created.

    ending:
        Done, on the last step, ends the walkthrough, leaving the chat input
        on the Chain tab, as it starts, with keyboard focus in its text box.
        Skip tour ends it straight away, at any step, leaving everything as
        it is. Either way the dimming goes, and the walkthrough is remembered
        as taken for the user, as the @{UserPreferencesScope} says, so it is
        never offered again by itself.

    starting:
        The walkthrough starts by itself only once for a user, until it has
        been taken or skipped: when the @{WelcomeScope}'s Get started is
        pressed, or, where the welcome page doesn't open at launch because
        everything is ready, once the window has opened. It can be taken
        again at any time with the Walkthrough command, a "Walkthrough"
        button with a signpost icon in the Help group of the
        @{RibbonApplicationTabScope}, after Welcome, whose tooltip says it
        walks through creating a project and the prompt modes. It is a full
        button, and not primary. Started with a project open, it starts at
        its first step all the same, offering "Use the open project" at the
        second.

        It never starts over an inset panel, but waits for it to close, and
        it isn't offered while work is running; started from its command, it
        closes any inset panel open first.

content.text:
I've specced a guided walkthrough: it starts on the Project tab, has you create a project, then explains Code, Spec, Code + Spec and Ask one at a time. `piton check` reports no problems, all changed files are formatted, and `piton build` succeeds. I confirmed the new scope and the ribbon changes in the refreshed reference.

**How it looks:** each step dims the window except for a cut-out around the part it's explaining. The cut-out is outlined in the theme's accent and glides to the next part over 200 ms. A callout card sits beside it with a title, a short explanation, "Step N of M", **Back**, **Next** (which reads **Done** on the last step) and **Skip tour**. Clicks on the dimmed area do nothing. Esc skips the tour, and Enter goes to the next step.

**The steps:**
1. **Projects live here:** opens the Project tab. A project is a folder with its spec, its code and a `piton.config.pi`.
2. **Create a project:** lights up New Project. It moves on by itself once the New Project form opens. If a project is already open, the callout also offers **Use the open project**, which skips to the modes.
3. **Fill it in:** lights up the New Project form, briefly explains the name, location, template and agents, and says the defaults are fine. It moves on by itself once the project is created. Cancelling goes back a step.
4. **Every prompt has a mode:** lights up the chat input's tabs.
5. **Code:** selects the Code tab. Changes the code to match the spec and runs on your machine.
6. **Spec:** selects the Spec tab. Changes only the spec, so you can agree on a change before anything is built. Runs in a container and builds the spec afterwards.
7. **Code and Spec:** selects the Chain tab. Updates the spec first, then a code step matches it. It's the default tab and the usual way to ask for a change.
8. **Ask:** selects the Ask tab. Questions change nothing, run straight away and are answered beside the tasks.
9. **You're ready:** lights up the text box, and mentions where to take the walkthrough again.

Each mode's step is drawn in that mode's colour. Back never returns to the project-creation steps once the project exists, and the walkthrough never sends a prompt.

**Starting and ending:**
- It starts by itself once per user: after **Get started** on the Welcome page, or at launch when everything is already ready and the Welcome page doesn't open.
- A new **Walkthrough** button follows Welcome in the Application tab's Help group.
- It waits for any open floating panel to close, and isn't offered while work is running.
- **Done** leaves the chat input on Chain with focus in the text box. Done or Skip marks it as taken, so it isn't offered again.

Choices you may want to change:
- **Freeform:** I left it out of the tour, since you listed four modes.
- **Accidental exits:** clicks outside the callout are ignored, so the tour can't end by accident. Only Skip tour or Esc ends it.

## What changed in the spec, and the anchors the code should follow

- **New `spec/scope/walkthrough/index.pi` (`WalkthroughScope`):**
  - **`WalkthroughShape.spotlight`:** a dimmed overlay with a cut-out (4 px of room, 6 px corners, accent outline) easing between targets over 200 ms. A callout card at most 320 px wide, with corners rounded 8 px and a pointer toward the target, placed where it fits. Only the callout and the target take input, Esc skips and Enter goes next.
  - **`WalkthroughShape.steps`:**
    - The nine steps in order.
    - Before showing each step, select its target: open the Project tab, expanding the ribbon if collapsed, or select the chat input tab.
    - Move on automatically when the New Project form opens and again when the project opens. Cancelling the form goes back a step.
    - Offer "Use the open project" when a project is already open.
    - Colour each mode step in its mode's colour. Back never re-enters the creation steps after the project is created.
  - **`WalkthroughShape.ending`:** Done selects Chain and focuses the text box. Done or Skip saves the "taken" preference.
  - **`WalkthroughShape.starting`:** auto-start once, after the Welcome page's Get started or at launch when the Welcome page doesn't open. Wait for any inset panel to close first and don't start while work is running. Starting from the command closes any open panel first.
- **`RibbonApplicationTabShape.groups.help`** and **`.commands.walkthrough`:** a full, non-primary "Walkthrough" button with a signpost icon, after Welcome.
- **`WelcomeShape.ready`:** Get started closes the page, then starts the walkthrough if it hasn't been taken.
- **`UserPreferencesShape.preferences`:** add "walkthrough taken or skipped", which starts as not taken.
